newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Party orders Plavsic to obey or resign.
newsitem.headline: Party orders Plavsic to obey or resign.

text.p: The Bosnian Serb republic's ruling SDS party warned President Biljana Plavsic on Tuesday that she would be ousted unless she obeyed its government, which is dominated by hardliners who are obstructing the Bosnian peace process.
The party leadership said Plavsic should comply or hand over power to Vice-President Dragoljub Mirjanic until the Bosnian Serb parliament, due to meet on Friday, removed her from power.

The SDS, which is covertly led by former president Radovan Karadzic, an indicted war criminal, said Plavsic acted unconstitutionally when she tried to sack the country's police chief in a crackdown on government corruption.
Plavsic was elected president last year when the international community forced Karadzic to renounce public office although it has not been able to prevent him wielding power behind the scenes.
Political sources said it would be a setback for the fragile peace process if Karadzic succeeded in toppling Plavsic, a wartime hardliner who has since become more moderate.

Plavsic, apparently aware that powerful hardliners would try to oust her, told a news conference in her northern industrial base of Banja Luka earlier: "There is no budget in the Bosnian Serb republic. The police are smuggling, the people are in misery and the country is isolated."

Relations between Plavsic and the hardliners reached a crisis at the weekend when she tried to dismiss police chief Dragan Kijac as interior minister for refusing the investigate suspect companies run by Karadzic and senior official Momcilo Krajisnik.
Although technically the Bosnian Serb head of state, she was briefly held by Yugoslav and Bosnian Serb police on Sunday when she returned early from a visit to London to deal with the dispute.

Plavsic told reporters that she was systematically excluded from decision-making by hardliners based in Pale outside Sarajevo and she was denied the cooperation of key government ministers like Kijac, who are loyal to Karadzic.

The political battle between Serbs pits pragmatists who support some cooperation with international peacemakers against ultra-nationalist diehards opposed to a postwar settlement that has denied Bosnian Serbs the outright independence they fought for.
Under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement engineered by the United States, the Bosnian Serb republic has an uneasy semi-autonomous status in Bosnia alongside a Moslem-Croat federation based in Sarajevo.
Karadzic and other wartime leaders have also clung to lucrative control of the local economy through their dominance of the SDS and the Bosnian Serb police.

Plavsic warned the hardliners that their defiance of the peace agreement could backfire with "the international community taking the simple way out and forcing the Bosnian Serb republic into a unitary Bosnia, which would be a disaster for us."
She added: "We have to go out into the world and cooperate with the world."
